operationalization: One could code historical biological publications for reliance on selection language and for subsequent physical-mechanistic investigation, but neither category supplies a non-arbitrary measure of inquiry being held back.
obstacles: The counterfactual amount of inquiry without the hypotheses is unobservable.
Key terms such as sufficient explanation and real cause are normative.
rationale: Bibliometric proxies are possible, but they substantially reinterpret the claim and cannot identify the proposed inhibition. Publication corpora also cover only part of biology and do not distinguish intellectual causation from changing methods or funding.

operationalization: For selected structures, fit physical models to measured material properties, forces, growth fields and resulting shapes, then compare predictions with observed morphogenesis. Agreement would support physical shaping in those cases, while systematic shape changes incompatible with the measured dynamics would refute the selected model but not the universal assertion.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public developmental imaging data for quantifying cell, tissue and organ shape changes.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D morphology for testing physical models of shells, bones and other structures.

obstacles: The claim ranges over all organisms and structural parts.
Observing compliance with physical law does not isolate which forces generated a form.
rationale: Many local physical models can be tested with existing imaging and morphology, but no dataset matches the universal scope. The statement is also close to a general physical commitment, making decisive discrimination from rivals difficult.

operationalization: No observation provides a unique criterion for whether morphology is, in the first instance, a mathematical or physical science rather than a biological science that uses those tools.
obstacles: The disciplinary classification is conceptual.
Any morphology can be described mathematically without establishing explanatory priority.
rationale: The claim concerns how a field and its problems should be classified. Existing datasets can test particular growth models, but cannot confirm or refute the stated disciplinary identity.

operationalization: Audit well-measured physiological processes for reproducible violations of conservation laws or established chemical and transport laws after closing their mass and energy budgets. A robust closed-system violation would refute the claim, but repeated compliance in sampled systems cannot confirm its unrestricted scope.

candidate_datasets.name: PhysioNet
candidate_datasets.role: Open physiological recordings for testing quantitative physical constraints in selected bodily systems.

obstacles: No finite dataset covers every organism and physical law.
Apparent violations commonly reflect unmeasured fluxes or model error.
rationale: Selected mechanisms can be checked against physical constraints, but the universal negative is not confirmable from datasets. Existing physiological records rarely include complete system boundaries needed for strong conservation tests.

operationalization: For structures with known material properties and boundary conditions, infer stresses or forces from shape and compare them with independently measured force fields. Accurate out-of-sample recovery would support the diagram-of-forces reading; non-unique or inaccurate recovery would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-resolved cell and tissue images from which shapes and deformation fields can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D biological forms for restricted biomechanical inverse analyses.

obstacles: Inverse mechanics is often non-identifiable from shape alone.
Material properties and boundary conditions are usually absent.
rationale: Modern inverse-mechanics methods make the idea measurable in selected systems, although mapping Thompson's forces to current variables requires interpretation. Shape alone generally admits several force histories, sharply limiting discrimination and full-scope adequacy.

operationalization: Measure amoeboid cell boundary curvature and shape as the contacting medium changes, estimate cortical or interfacial tension, and test whether tension predicts the deformation after controlling for active cytoskeletal forces. A reproducible medium-dependent tension-shape relation would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy of cells, including amoeboid forms, for boundary-shape measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy datasets that may pair perturbations with cell-shape dynamics.

obstacles: Historical surface tension maps imperfectly to active cortical tension.
Most image datasets lack independent force measurements.
rationale: The claim has measurable variables and perturbation-based tests, but public datasets rarely contain tension, medium and shape together. Available imaging can resolve the shape component and selected mechanisms, not the full causal generalization.

operationalization: Estimate effective viscosity and viscoelastic relaxation from time-resolved amoeba deformation under known pressure or force, and compare flow and relaxation with water and high-viscosity reference fluids. Slow force-dependent flow with a much larger effective viscosity would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Microscopy sequences for quantifying amoeboid deformation and flow.

obstacles: Public images seldom include calibrated applied pressure.
Protoplasm is active and viscoelastic, not a passive Newtonian fluid.
rationale: The phenomenology maps well to standard rheological measurements, giving good operationalizability and discrimination. Existing public data are mostly imaging rather than complete force-response experiments, so only a restricted test is currently practical.

operationalization: No dataset can uniquely decide whether a phenomenon belongs to a clearly bounded vital or physical category without first imposing the classification whose absence the claim asserts.
obstacles: Vital is undefined.
The asserted lack of a clean taxonomy is methodological rather than observational.
rationale: This is a conceptual claim about classification and research strategy. Particular processes can be physically modelled, but their success cannot establish that no clear global division exists.

operationalization: One could measure energy use and force generation during fertilization, chromosome motion and development, but the assertion that matter acts only as a seat of energy or centre of force has no distinct outcome from ordinary physical descriptions of matter.
obstacles: Seats of energy and centres of force lack unique modern measurements.
The word only makes the framing metaphysical rather than a separable mechanism.
rationale: Developmental datasets document chromosome dynamics and energetics, yet all outcomes can be redescribed in the claim's terms. It therefore supplies no discriminating empirical criterion as stated.

operationalization: Using repeated or cross-sectional length and weight records, compute k = W/L^3 and test whether it is constant over size or age. Stable k supports geometric similarity at roughly constant density; systematic k changes refute unchanged form or density and can be compared with direct shape data.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Public species-level length-weight relationships for testing departures from cubic scaling.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries Data Catalog
candidate_datasets.role: Survey datasets with fish length, weight, species and sampling metadata.

obstacles: Changes in density can alter k without shape change.
Cross-sectional records can confound growth with cohort or sex.
rationale: The equation, variables and decision criterion are explicit, and large public fish survey data contain the needed measurements. Direct morphometrics would strengthen attribution specifically to form, but the core relationship is readily testable.

operationalization: Fit log trunk diameter against log height within and across tree species and test whether the slope is 1.5, then evaluate buckling safety factors using wood density and elastic modulus. Strongly different slopes or trees stable beyond the predicted buckling boundary would refute the stated law.

candidate_datasets.name: ForestGEO
candidate_datasets.role: Long-term tree censuses with stem diameter and species across forest plots.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant traits including height and wood properties for allometric tests.

obstacles: Diameter and height are not always measured together openly.
Taper, branching, wind loading and species-specific wood properties violate homogeneity.
rationale: The exponent is directly testable, and substantial tree trait and census data exist. Testing the exact buckling explanation and maximum height requires harmonizing mechanical traits and architecture, while the law's homogeneous-body assumptions restrict applicability.

operationalization: Estimate limb-bone cross-sectional area, body mass, muscle area and locomotor performance across terrestrial species, test the predicted square-cube scaling, and calculate safety factors and failure thresholds. Departure from the proposed scaling or viable taxa beyond the predicted bound would count against the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D skeletal scans for limb cross-sections and geometric scaling.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Public mammalian body-size and life-history traits for comparative analyses.

obstacles: No observed fauna samples the counterfactual sizes near a universal failure limit.
Posture, gait, bone geometry and material properties confound simple square-cube scaling.
rationale: Existing morphology and trait data can test scaling and estimate mechanical margins across many terrestrial mammals. They cannot cleanly establish a definite universal maximum, because lineages alter posture and structure and because extinct giants require incomplete fossil reconstructions.

operationalization: Compare maximum body size and structural safety factors across neutrally buoyant aquatic and terrestrial taxa, and model how buoyancy changes skeletal loading. Evidence that another physical constraint imposes a finite aquatic size bound would refute indefinite physical growth, while reduced gravity loading alone supports only the narrower premise.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Maximum length and ecology across fishes for aquatic size distributions.

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: Public marine species occurrence and trait-linked records for broad taxonomic coverage.

obstacles: Indefinite growth is an unobservable limiting assertion.
Hydrodynamic, feeding, oxygen and tissue constraints remain despite buoyancy.
rationale: Public trait data and mechanics can establish that buoyancy relaxes weight support, but cannot confirm absence of every physical barrier. The strongest empirical test addresses a restricted interpretation rather than literal indefinite growth.

operationalization: Within closely related fishes, regress burst speed, fatigue time and annual movement distance on body length while controlling temperature and ecology, and compare exponents with the square-cube predictions. Larger fish lacking higher burst speed, or annual distance increasing strongly with size, would refute components of the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Public animal tracking studies that can estimate movement speed and annual distance for selected fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Body size, ecology and some swimming-related species information.

obstacles: Burst speed and fatigue are rarely paired with annual tracking in the same individuals.
Temperature, swimming mode and tag effects confound size comparisons.
rationale: The predictions are explicit and can be tested for selected species, but the required performance and long-term movement variables are fragmented. A small team could resolve individual components, not the full joint scaling claim.

operationalization: Across geometrically similar birds, fit minimum sustained flight speed and flight power against linear size and test exponents of 0.5 and 3.5, while comparing available muscle power with an exponent of 3. Deviations outside uncertainty or successful flight above the predicted power margin would refute the model.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Public tracking and accelerometry studies for flight speed in multiple bird species.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Open global bird morphology and mass traits for body-size and wing-form covariates.

obstacles: Flight power and muscle power are seldom directly measured in open comparative datasets.
Bird proportions and flight styles are not fixed across size.
rationale: The scaling exponents give clear tests and open morphology plus movement data cover many birds. The exact energetic quantities require model-derived estimates and harmonization, so the claim is currently resolvable only under subsets and assumptions.

operationalization: Reconstruct body mass, wing area, muscle capacity and required flight power for ostrich, moa and comparably large flying birds, then test whether required power exceeds physiologically plausible muscle output under ordinary avian anatomy. A feasible positive power margin would refute physiological impossibility.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D skeletal scans of living and fossil birds for anatomical reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative measurements of extant bird mass, wings and morphology.

obstacles: Moa soft tissue and wing anatomy require uncertain reconstruction.
Extant ratites' reduced wings reflect evolutionary history as well as size.
rationale: Biomechanical feasibility can be estimated with public scans and comparative traits, especially for the man-sized prediction. The categorical historical claims remain sensitive to uncertain soft tissues and what counts as ordinary anatomy.

operationalization: Combine fossil body and wing reconstructions with independent proxy estimates of atmospheric pressure and composition, then model whether inferred density was required for flight. Modern-density mechanical feasibility or proxies excluding notably greater density would refute the proposed explanation.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrence and taxonomic records for giant insects and pterosaurs.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA World Data Service for Paleoclimatology
candidate_datasets.role: Public paleoclimate and geochemical proxy data relevant to ancient atmospheric conditions.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil scans for reconstructing flight morphology.

obstacles: Ancient total atmospheric pressure is poorly constrained.
Fossil deformation and missing soft tissues affect aerodynamic estimates.
High oxygen, not carbon dioxide, is a major rival explanation for insect gigantism.
rationale: The historical hypothesis has measurable fossil and geochemical consequences and relevant public repositories exist. Sparse atmospheric proxies and uncertain flight reconstructions limit a clean causal test, although substantial parts can be evaluated now.

operationalization: Compile maximal jump height, body length and limb geometry for similarly constructed animals, then test whether absolute height has a size exponent of zero after controlling lever ratios. A consistent nonzero scaling exponent would refute the stated law.

candidate_datasets.name: AnimalTraits
candidate_datasets.role: Open animal trait records that can support comparative locomotor-performance compilation.

obstacles: Jump-height measurements are sparse and methodologically heterogeneous.
Finding animals that satisfy similar construction across a wide size range is difficult.
rationale: The predicted exponent and outcome are unambiguous, and published public trait records permit a restricted comparative test. Coverage from fleas to horses with matched geometry is inadequate, requiring substantial compilation for the full scope.

operationalization: Within each locomotor mode and among similarly constructed species, regress characteristic velocity on linear size and test whether the exponent is 0.5. Mode-specific exponents significantly different from one-half would refute the claimed common result.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Public tracking data for estimating walking, swimming and flight speeds.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Bird morphology and mass for flight scaling analyses.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Fish lengths and ecological traits for swimming comparisons.

obstacles: Characteristic speed must be standardized across tracking studies.
Construction, behavior and environment covary strongly with size.
rationale: The exponent is directly estimable with standard allometric models, and large open movement and trait resources exist. Coverage and standardization are uneven across all three modes, and the similar-construction condition reduces effective sample size.

operationalization: A direct test would compare terrestrial lineages evolving or developing under otherwise similar but different gravity, measuring posture, limb length, locomotor performance and cardiopulmonary investment. Existing Earth data can test gravity-load mechanics but not the predicted whole-fauna response to doubled or halved gravity.

candidate_datasets.name: NASA Open Science Data Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Public spaceflight and altered-gravity biological data, chiefly for short-term organismal responses.

obstacles: No population-level vertebrate dataset spans long-term evolution under doubled gravity.
Spaceflight data mostly concern microgravity, short duration and limited taxa.
Predictions such as failure and resemble are qualitative.
rationale: The claim has measurable consequences after substantial interpretation, but the decisive counterfactual gravity regimes have not been observed over development and evolution. Existing altered-gravity data are too restricted to resolve the stated terrestrial morphology predictions.

operationalization: Measure internal surface area and body or organ mass across sizes for gut, spiral valve and cortex, then test whether folding maintains an approximately constant surface-to-mass ratio and whether fold complexity rises as predicted. Declining ratios despite folds or absent size-complexity associations would refute components.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Open brain imaging and anatomy data for cortical surface and volume measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D anatomical scans for comparative internal-surface morphology.

obstacles: Surface area is rarely annotated directly.
Different organs and taxa require incompatible imaging and segmentation.
Maintaining function rather than a constant geometric ratio is a plausible rival.
rationale: Modern 3D data permit tests for selected organs and taxa, and the scaling criterion is measurable. Existing datasets do not provide comparable surface and mass measurements across the broad morphological scope.

operationalization: Across organism sizes, quantify deviation from spherical or capillary-equilibrium shapes and compare estimated capillary and gravitational stresses using Bond numbers and perturbation data. Small forms insensitive to gravity but predictably altered by interfacial or cortical tension would support the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public cell and microorganism images for shape quantification.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Microscopy datasets for comparing shapes across perturbations and scales.

obstacles: Active cytoskeletal forces can mimic tension-driven shapes.
Most datasets lack measured tension and gravity perturbations.
All small organisms is an exceptionally broad scope.
rationale: The gravity-versus-tension prediction can be formalized and tested in selected cells or microorganisms. Public imaging is abundant but force metadata and taxonomic breadth are insufficient for the universal mechanistic claim.

operationalization: Infer directional growth fields from time-lapse imaging and test whether they predict shape change in large organisms but fail in minute organisms, where measured cortical or interfacial forces should instead predict form. Cross-scale predictive comparisons would support or refute the proposed dichotomy.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse developmental imaging across cells, tissues and embryos.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Microscopy of individual cells and microorganisms for minute-scale shape dynamics.

obstacles: Large and minute lack a stated threshold.
Growth and active molecular forces jointly determine form at both scales.
Comparable force and growth fields are rarely available.
rationale: Existing time-lapse imaging can test the growth-form relation in exemplar systems. The asserted categorical scale split requires substantial modern interpretation and broad matched data that do not currently exist.

operationalization: Segment cells through growth and division, calculate surface-area-to-volume ratios before and after cytokinesis, and test whether division restores a characteristic ratio without changing total volume. The geometric component is supported by an increased total surface and restored ratio, but the proposed energy-balance cause requires independent energetic measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse 3D microscopy of cell division and embryonic cleavage.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public division imagery for cell geometry measurements.

obstacles: Segmentation resolution limits true membrane surface estimates.
Geometry alone cannot identify surface-energy balance as the cause of division.
rationale: The surface-to-volume consequence is straightforward to test with existing 3D images and standard segmentation. The mechanistic claim that division restores an energy balance is much less discriminating and usually lacks the necessary energetic data.

operationalization: Measure volumes of matched cell types across dwarf, normal and giant individuals and regress cell size and cell number on body size. Nearly invariant cell size with number accounting for body-size differences supports the claim; strong within-type cell-size scaling refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Open tissue microscopy for measuring cell dimensions across tissue types.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public comparative microscopy datasets with cellular resolution.

obstacles: Matched body-size phenotypes and cell types are uncommon in one dataset.
Cell volume estimates depend on tissue preparation and segmentation.
Some tissues vary by ploidy or hypertrophy.
rationale: The variables and refuting pattern are clear, and extensive cellular images exist. However, data directly pairing individual body size, cell size and cell number across the claimed taxa and phenotypes are incomplete, so the broad law is only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Across species, measure homologous ganglion-cell volumes and total cell counts per ganglion, then test whether cell size varies narrowly while ganglion cell number rises with species body size. Broad neuron-size scaling or no number-size association would refute the generalization.

candidate_datasets.name: NeuroMorpho.Org
candidate_datasets.role: Open neuronal reconstructions across species for cell morphology and size.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Open comparative brain and cell-type data for selected species.

obstacles: Homologous ganglia and neuron classes are difficult to align across phyla.
Repositories emphasize selected neurons rather than unbiased cell counts.
Body-size metadata are often missing.
rationale: Neuron dimensions and cell counts are measurable and existing neuroanatomical resources support restricted comparisons. Taxonomic selection, missing ganglion totals and uncertain homology prevent resolution of the asserted general law.

operationalization: Compile verified dimensions, genome sizes and molecular inventories of the smallest free-living and host-dependent organisms, estimate the minimum components required for autonomous life, and compare discovered cells with that bound. Organisms substantially below the proposed scale would refute the historical prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Public bacterial and archaeal phenotypes, including cell morphology and dimensions for many strains.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Genome
candidate_datasets.role: Public genome assemblies and sizes for microorganisms.

obstacles: Reported ultramicrobe sizes can reflect filtration artifacts or nonliving particles.
Dependence on hosts blurs the definition of organism and minimum autonomous machinery.
rationale: Modern cell-size and genome data can directly evaluate whether known organisms approach a plausible molecular lower bound and whether much smaller forms have been found. The phrase cannot be much smaller remains imprecise, and completeness of discovery cannot be guaranteed.

operationalization: Estimate spatial directional growth tensors from longitudinal images and test whether integrating their ratios predicts observed external shape trajectories. Predictive failure after measured growth is supplied would refute the relation in a system, while success across diverse taxa would support its restricted form.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-resolved developmental images for estimating directional growth and shape.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D morphology at multiple stages for selected organisms.

obstacles: Most morphology datasets are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal.
Growth ratios can describe shape change without identifying its cause.
The scope covers nearly all organisms.
rationale: Directional growth and external form are measurable with modern imaging, but Thompson's universal accounting claim exceeds available taxonomic and temporal coverage. Existing data can resolve it in selected developmental systems only.

operationalization: From longitudinal 3D landmarks, estimate directional growth-rate ratios and shape coordinates over time. Constant ratios accompanied by stable shape and ratio changes preceding persistent shape change support the claim; dissociation between these variables refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Longitudinal embryo and tissue imaging for growth and shape trajectories.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Ontogenetic 3D specimens for growth-form comparisons.

obstacles: The seasonal-duration assertion needs long time series rarely available.
Cross-sectional ontogenetic series can confound individual growth with variation.
rationale: The core geometry yields a clear longitudinal test with standard morphometrics. Public imaging can resolve selected organisms, but broad claims about multicellular organisms and duration beyond a season lack matched coverage.

operationalization: Use time-lapse vertebrate embryo images to map local tissue growth and deformation before and during neural and amniotic folding, then fit mechanical sheet models. Spatially patterned growth that predicts fold initiation supports the mechanism; folding without the necessary differential growth or better prediction by active bending alone refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open time-lapse embryonic imaging suitable for cell tracking, growth maps and fold dynamics.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public multidimensional biological imaging, including developmental studies.

obstacles: Growth, cell-shape change and active contractility can be difficult to separate.
Amniotic-fold coverage is less abundant than neural-fold imaging.
rationale: Modern live imaging and tissue mechanics directly expose the variables and allow rival models to be compared. Existing open developmental datasets and standard tracking methods can test the mechanism in representative vertebrate embryos now.

operationalization: Measure pairwise morphological and size disparity between related taxa at matched embryonic, fetal and adult stages, and test whether disparity generally increases with developmental time. Large early-stage differences or decreasing disparity toward adulthood would refute the prediction for those pairs.

candidate_datasets.name: e-Mouse Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D mouse developmental anatomy for stage-specific morphology.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative developmental imaging for selected species and stages.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D ontogenetic specimens across vertebrate taxa.

obstacles: Comparable stages and structures across species are difficult to align.
Embryos of related species are unevenly sampled.
Development can include early divergence followed by convergence.
rationale: Developmental disparity is directly measurable, and open image repositories provide useful series for selected vertebrate clades. Coverage is insufficient for the universal any-two-related-forms wording and comparative staging introduces substantial judgment.

operationalization: Fit age-specific height and height-velocity curves from longitudinal or repeated cross-sectional measurements from birth to adulthood. The claimed sequence is confirmed by an infant peak, slower childhood interval, adolescent acceleration and approach to zero velocity, and refuted if those phases are absent.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Public measured stature and age data for children and adults.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Public longitudinal and cross-sectional growth standards for early childhood.

obstacles: Cross-sectional surveys smooth individual timing.
Sex and population differences require stratification.
rationale: The variables and phases are standard, with large public datasets covering the relevant ages. Standard spline or growth-curve analyses can decisively assess the empirical pattern within days.

operationalization: Estimate measured standing height by age in adulthood, preferably longitudinally, and test whether decline begins before 50 and is appreciable by 60 and extreme old age. Stable stature through those ages would refute the timing and magnitude claims.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Public measured adult stature across a wide age range.

candidate_datasets.name: Health and Retirement Study
candidate_datasets.role: Public longitudinal aging data including physical measurements for older adults.

obstacles: Cross-sectional age differences include cohort effects.
Posture and vertebral compression affect standing height measurement.
rationale: Adult stature and age are directly measured in large public studies, and the age trend has an explicit refuting pattern. Longitudinal aging data can separate within-person loss from cohort differences sufficiently to resolve the claim.

operationalization: Fit log body weight against log stature through growth and test whether the exponent is near three, with deviations attributable to changing shape or density. An exponent materially different from three or systematic residual trends would refute strict cubic similarity.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Public measured height, weight, age and sex for growth allometry.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Public child length, height and weight reference data.

obstacles: Human proportions and tissue composition change with age.
Repeated cross-sections are not individual trajectories.
rationale: Large open anthropometric datasets directly contain the variables across growth. A standard allometric regression cleanly tests the cubic tendency and quantifies the stated qualifications.

operationalization: Estimate sex-specific height-velocity curves and compare their shapes after allowing amplitude and time shifts. Similar aligned curves with an earlier female adolescent acceleration support the claim; irreconcilable shape differences or no phase lead refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Public sex-, age- and stature data for estimating population growth curves.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Growth Reference 5–19 years
candidate_datasets.role: Public sex-specific growth reference data through adolescence.

obstacles: Velocity from cross-sectional data is model-derived.
Pubertal timing varies across populations and cohorts.
rationale: The phase and amplitude comparison is explicit and uses standard growth-curve methods. Large public sex-stratified anthropometric datasets span childhood and adolescence and are adequate for a decisive present-day test.

operationalization: Fit size-at-age and growth-velocity curves from birth or hatching to adulthood across animal taxa, then test for the shared sequence of slow onset, early velocity maximum and terminal slowdown. Taxa with maximal growth late or persistent nonzero adult growth would refute universality.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge
candidate_datasets.role: Public animal life-history and growth-related records across many species.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Growth parameters and size information for many fishes.

obstacles: Comparable raw longitudinal growth curves are scattered.
Birth, hatching and growth cessation differ fundamentally across taxa.
The universal wording is vulnerable to poorly sampled exceptions.
rationale: The phase sequence is measurable, and open databases permit broad tests for selected vertebrates. Existing standardized trajectories do not cover animals generally, so the universal generalization cannot be fully resolved without major compilation.

operationalization: Fit asymptotic and determinate growth models to long-term size-at-age data for ectotherms, especially fishes, and compare predictive fit and late-life growth estimates. Observed cessation at a fixed adult size or consistently superior non-asymptotic models would refute the generalization.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Public von Bertalanffy growth parameters and maximum sizes for numerous fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries Data Catalog
candidate_datasets.role: Public long-running fish surveys with age and size measurements.

obstacles: Old individuals are under-sampled because of mortality and fishing.
Apparent asymptotes may reflect selective disappearance rather than individual growth.
rationale: Long-running fish surveys and compiled growth parameters directly support model comparison across many species. Sampling biases remain, but the stated asymptotic pattern and alternatives are distinguishable with standard methods.

operationalization: Decompose adult size across species into fitted growth rate and duration parameters, then test whether both independently explain final size and whether rabbit–guinea-pig and human–rabbit contrasts follow the stated components. Failure of either component to predict size would refute that part.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge
candidate_datasets.role: Public mammalian development, maturity, adult mass and longevity traits.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Public mammalian life-history and body-size traits for comparative analysis.

obstacles: Databases contain endpoints more often than complete growth trajectories.
Growth rate and duration estimates are statistically correlated.
Phylogeny and ecology confound three-species comparisons.
rationale: The decomposition is measurable and can be tested for mammals using public life-history data plus published trajectories. The broad animal scope and lack of standardized curve parameters across species make the full claim only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Fit fetal length against gestational age with a smooth curve and locate the maximum first derivative or zero second derivative. A velocity peak near gestational month five supports the claim; a well-estimated peak at a materially different time or monotonic velocity refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: INTERGROWTH-21st
candidate_datasets.role: Public international fetal growth standards and longitudinal ultrasound measurements.

obstacles: Ultrasound commonly measures crown-rump length only early and long-bone dimensions later.
Gestational dating and choice of length proxy affect inflection estimates.
rationale: Gestational age and fetal linear dimensions are available in modern longitudinal growth resources. Standard smooth growth models can estimate the timing of peak velocity, though harmonizing length measures introduces some uncertainty.

operationalization: At each age, estimate mean growth velocity and the coefficient of variation in height and weight, then test whether variability declines during slower childhood growth and rises during adolescent acceleration. Weak, reversed or absent age-specific association would refute the proposed relation.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Large public age-specific height and weight samples for variability curves.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Growth Reference 5–19 years
candidate_datasets.role: Sex-specific growth distributions spanning childhood and adolescence.

obstacles: Population heterogeneity in pubertal timing can itself inflate variability.
Association does not establish that growth rate causes variability.
rationale: Public anthropometric samples are sufficiently large to estimate age-specific means, variances and velocities. They can resolve the empirical tracking claim, although causal interpretation remains confounded by maturation timing.

operationalization: Fit segmented growth curves around independently dated birth, puberty and metamorphic transitions and test for discontinuities or slope changes. Smooth trajectories through those epochs would refute the corresponding component.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Human anthropometry around childhood and puberty.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental imaging series that include metamorphic or embryonic transitions in selected animals.

obstacles: Puberty and metamorphosis timing must be measured independently of growth.
Comparable longitudinal mass or size series are sparse outside model species.
rationale: Change-point analysis gives a direct test and rich human data cover birth and adolescence. Existing open data can test selected metamorphosing taxa, but not the broad assertion across animals.

operationalization: Measure the same individuals' wet or dry mass immediately before and after metamorphosis across eels, insects and amphibians. Frequent mass loss supports often, while a well-sampled class showing stable or increased mass would refute always.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Public ecological and developmental datasets containing stage-specific body mass for selected metamorphosing species.

obstacles: Relevant measurements are scattered rather than standardized.
Hydration and gut evacuation can mimic tissue loss.
Often has no explicit frequency threshold.
rationale: The pre/post mass contrast is simple and highly discriminating. Public datasets can test representative species and readily challenge the universal extension, but taxonomically broad paired measurements require substantial compilation.

operationalization: Estimate organ-to-body mass or volume ratios across age and test whether ratios remain constant; for brain, compare the ratio at birth and age 25 with the stated approximate fractions. Significant age-dependent allometry supports the central claim, while constant ratios refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NIH Pediatric MRI Data Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Public pediatric brain imaging and demographic data for brain-volume growth.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Connectome Project
candidate_datasets.role: Open young-adult brain imaging for adult brain volumes.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: Public age-specific body measurements for denominator estimates.

obstacles: Combining repositories introduces cohort and measurement differences.
Historical fractions may depend on mass-versus-volume conversion.
rationale: Age, body size and organ volumes are well-defined, and public human imaging spans key developmental periods. Standard allometric models can decisively test non-constant organ ratios, even if the exact historical fractions carry measurement uncertainty.

operationalization: For plaice records, calculate k = W/L^3, model it flexibly against length, and locate its maximum relative to independently measured maturity size. Constant or monotonic k, or a peak far from approximately 30 cm and maturity onset, would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Public ICES trawl-survey fish measurements, including plaice length and biological observations.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Plaice length-weight and maturity information for comparison.

obstacles: Sex, season and stock alter condition and maturity size.
Some survey records lack individual weight or maturity.
rationale: The taxon, equation, curve shape and approximate peak are explicit. Large public fisheries records permit a rapid stratified test with sufficient size coverage and independent maturity information.

operationalization: Model plaice weight conditional on length, month, gonad stage and tissue condition, testing for the stated winter decline and summer-autumn recovery. Mediation by gonad and spawning status supports the mechanism; persistence after reproductive controls or stronger environmental predictors refutes the claim that spawning wholly causes it.

candidate_datasets.name: DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Public seasonal survey records for plaice length, weight, sex and biological state.

candidate_datasets.name: ICES Data Portal
candidate_datasets.role: Public fisheries and ecosystem data for seasonal and environmental covariates.

obstacles: Survey timing and fields vary among cruises.
Food availability and temperature covary with spawning season.
Wholly is difficult to establish observationally.
rationale: Seasonal condition at fixed length can be estimated from extensive public fish surveys. Reproductive-stage fields and environmental covariates allow a strong, though not perfectly experimental, test of both pattern and exclusive mechanism.

operationalization: Estimate organ-specific growth trajectories and test whether their relative rates predict species- or genotype-specific adult morphology. Perturbations or natural variants that change local rates and produce the predicted form differences would support causality; unchanged morphology would refute it in that system.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-resolved organism and organ development images for local growth estimates.

candidate_datasets.name: e-Mouse Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Stage-resolved 3D mouse anatomy for organ-specific growth trajectories.

obstacles: Specific morphology and large part lack quantitative thresholds.
Local growth can be consequence as well as cause of patterning.
Comparable trajectories across taxa are sparse.
rationale: Heterochrony and organ-specific growth are measurable in model organisms, with public developmental atlases supporting restricted tests. The broad causal contribution to multicellular morphology is too vague and taxonomically expansive for full resolution.

operationalization: For each species, fit root or shoot elongation across experimental temperatures and estimate the temperature of maximum growth, then compare temperate plants with maize, melon and other warm-climate plants. Broad dispersion among temperate optima or no warmer-climate shift would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant trait data that can help identify species and growth-related traits for comparative synthesis.

candidate_datasets.name: Environmental Data Initiative
candidate_datasets.role: Public ecological datasets that include plant growth under environmental gradients in selected studies.

obstacles: Temperature-response experiments are scattered and use different endpoints.
Optima depend on developmental stage, organ and acclimation.
TRY does not directly provide complete temperature-response curves for all species.
rationale: The optimum and group contrast are directly measurable, but no single open resource appears to contain standardized full response curves for the stated species scope. Existing public studies permit a subset test after harmonization.

operationalization: Fit growth or development rates across temperatures within normal ranges and calculate Q10 values, testing whether rates rise approximately exponentially and Q10 commonly lies between two and three. Systematic non-exponential responses or Q10 values outside that range would refute the stated law.

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
candidate_datasets.role: Open ecological time-series data with abundance and environmental context for selected temperature-related growth analyses.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Public experimental datasets containing organismal growth and development across temperatures.

obstacles: Relevant experiments require compilation from many deposits.
Q10 varies with temperature interval and proximity to thermal limits.
Field time series confound temperature with season.
rationale: The mathematical response and coefficient are explicit and widely measured, and open experimental data can support tests across representative plants and animals. Broad synthesis requires harmonization, but standard regressions can resolve the qualified claim with current data.

operationalization: Use time-resolved growth and damage or survival markers across temperatures to fit a model combining low-temperature kinetic acceleration with cumulative high-temperature injury, and compare it against a primary optimum-response model. Superior out-of-sample fit and temporal accumulation of damage would support the proposed resultant mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Public thermal-performance experiments for selected plants and animals.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public study datasets that may pair growth responses with molecular or physiological stress measurements.

obstacles: Growth and cumulative damage are rarely measured together.
Acclimation, enzyme kinetics and resource limitation produce similar optimum curves.
The proposed mechanism spans diverse processes and taxa.
rationale: Competing mechanistic models can be formulated and tested in systems with repeated thermal exposure and stress measurements. Existing public datasets are fragmented and usually resolve only selected organisms or proxy damage variables, limiting causal discrimination.
